title: What Manhood Is For
subtitle: A five-session study on masculinity, strength, and the man Jesus was.
summary:
This study is for men who are tired of being handed two masculinities and told to pick, the swaggering one that mistakes volume for strength and the soft one that mistakes absence for peace, and who suspect the truth is neither. It walks slowly through five sessions on what biblical manhood actually is once the culture-war caricatures are cleared away, on the father wound and the God who names himself Father of the fatherless, on strength under control in the man who wept and washed feet and drove the money changers out with a whip, on emotional honesty and friendship and the silence that is killing men who will not say they are drowning, and on servant leadership against domination, and the calling every man has to raise or mentor the next one. It is built so a busy man or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer rather than in the performance men so often bring into a room of other men.

This is not a study that stands over men and grades them. The writer came to faith out of atheism, was raised without a father, and is now raising five sons, and both of those last facts sit under every line. He knows the ache of a chair at the table that was always empty, and he knows the fear of a man who has no template for the thing he is trying to become for his boys. He does not write from a safe distance. He has been the man who confused controlling a room with leading it, who went silent for days rather than say he was afraid, who reached for anger because it felt more like strength than the truth did. He writes from inside the indictment, and so will you. And it refuses both counterfeits with equal force. It will not baptize the domineering man who reads Scripture as a permit for his temper, and it will not excuse the passive man who calls his absence humility. It holds up one man as the measure, the one who had all the strength there is and bent it entirely toward the good of the people in front of him.
audience: Men, fathers, sons, and the small groups and mentoring pairs that carry them

sessions.title: What Manhood Is For, Past the Caricatures
sessions.aim: To clear away the two culture-war caricatures of masculinity, the domineering strongman and the passive nice guy, and to recover manhood as something given by God for a purpose rather than proven against other men, refusing both the swagger that mistakes volume for strength and the softness that mistakes absence for peace.
sessions.summary: A young man told Bell he did not know how to be a man because everyone who had tried to tell him was selling something. One voice said a real man dominates, wins, never backs down, takes what he wants. The other said the whole idea was toxic and he should apologize for having shoulders. He was standing between two caricatures, and neither one was going to make him a man. The real question is not which team to join in the culture war over masculinity but what manhood is actually for, because you cannot become a thing you have only ever seen drawn as a cartoon. Scripture does not begin with conquest. It begins with a garden and a man placed in it to work it and to keep it, given labor and responsibility before any culture handed him a script. Bell takes the strong case for the recovery of masculine strength, the books and voices insisting that men were made for weight and risk and that the church has too often produced men who are merely harmless. There is real truth in it, and the passive man is a genuine problem, because the first failure of manhood in Scripture is not Cain's violence but Adam's silence, a man who stood right there and said nothing. But the recovery movement keeps sliding into the caricature it meant to correct, until strength means getting your way and manhood means never being crossed. Then the reversal. The first sin of the first man was passivity, and the loudest counterfeit of manhood is the fear of being weak dressed up as strength. Real manhood is neither the strongman nor the nice guy. It is strength given a purpose outside itself, the man who works and keeps, who takes responsibility no one assigned him, who is strong the way a roof is strong, for the sake of what it shelters.

keyScripture.why: Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love, placing the call to strength and the call to love in the same breath so that neither the strongman nor the nice guy can claim the verse, because Paul commands both at once and lets neither stand alone.

discussion.q: Bell says most of us learned manhood from two caricatures, the strongman who dominates and the nice guy who apologizes for existing, and that neither one makes a man. Which cartoon did you absorb, and where did you get it?
discussion.behind: Open by surfacing the script each man is running before defining anything. Most men have swallowed one caricature and are quietly ashamed they cannot pull it off, or have rejected one so hard they backed into the other. Do not resolve it yet. Just get the inherited picture out loud, and notice how often it came from a screen, a locker room, or a father, present or absent.

discussion.q: Scripture puts the first man in a garden to work it and keep it before it says one word about strength or authority. What changes when you hear that manhood starts with responsibility given, not dominance proven?
discussion.behind: Move to the theological ground. The culture defines a man by what he conquers or consumes. Genesis defines him by what he is charged to cultivate and protect. Help the room feel the relief and the weight of it at once, that manhood is a stewardship handed to you, not a rank you have to fight your way into against other men.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that the church has produced too many merely harmless men, and that the passive man is a real failure. Where have you called your own passivity peace, or humility, or picking your battles?
discussion.behind: Honor the truth in the recovery movement and then turn it inward. The first sin of the first man was silence, standing right there and saying nothing. Press gently on where each man goes quiet and calls it wisdom, avoids and calls it patience, disappears and calls it not wanting conflict. Go first and name your own retreat.

discussion.q: The same movement that names the passive man often slides into the strongman, until strength just means getting your way. Where have you confused being strong with being loud, being right, or never being crossed?
discussion.behind: Now turn the knife the other direction so the room cannot simply pick the strongman as the cure. The counterfeit strength is fragile, threatened by any challenge, needing the last word. Help men see that the man who cannot be contradicted is not strong but scared, and that the fear of looking weak is running the whole performance.

discussion.q: If manhood is strength given a purpose outside itself, like a roof that is strong for the sake of what it shelters, who and what is your strength actually for right now, and would they say they feel sheltered by it?
discussion.behind: Land the session on purpose, not on the culture war. Push each man past the abstract to the actual people under his roof, literal and otherwise. The test of a man's strength is not how much he has but what it is bent toward. Ask, gently, whether the people nearest him experience his strength as shelter or as weather they have to survive.

objections.objection: This whole conversation about masculinity is the problem. There is no such thing as biblical manhood, only human virtue, and telling men to be men just smuggles in a bunch of cultural stereotypes and dresses them up as Scripture.
objections.response: Grant a large piece of this, because a great deal of what gets sold as biblical manhood is exactly that, a mid-century cultural picture with a verse stapled on, the pickup truck and the grill and the refusal to cry treated as holiness. That is worth rejecting, and the study rejects it. But notice the overcorrection. Scripture does address men as men, tells them to act like men and be strong in the same breath it tells them to do everything in love, holds up specific men and specific failures of manhood, Adam's silence, David's abuse of power, as men. To flatten all of that into generic virtue is to lose something the text will not let us lose, that God made humanity male and female on purpose and calls each to a particular faithfulness. The answer to a bad picture of manhood is a true one, not no picture at all, because men who are told manhood means nothing do not become free. They become adrift, and someone worse is always waiting to hand them a counterfeit.

objections.objection: Real men lead, provide, and protect, and the reason the culture is falling apart is that men have gone soft. The church needs to stop apologizing and call men back to being strong, decisive, and in charge.
objections.response: Agree with the diagnosis and refuse the cure, because half of this is true and the half that is false is dangerous. Passivity is a real failure, the first one in Scripture, and a call to strength and courage is a call the Bible actually makes. But watch the words leading, providing, protecting collapse into being in charge, because that is where the strongman hides. The man Scripture holds up as the measure did lead and provide and protect, and he did it by washing feet, by weeping, by laying his life down, by using his strength entirely for the people in front of him and never once for himself. Strength is not the problem and softness is not the cure. The question is what the strength is for. A man strong for himself is not a leader, he is a hazard, and the culture is not falling apart for lack of men in charge. It is groaning under men who confused being in charge with being good.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If you are honest, are you more tempted to prove you are a man by dominating a room, or to avoid the risk of manhood by disappearing from it, and what are you afraid of underneath both?
sessions.practice: This week, catch yourself once in your default counterfeit. If you tend toward the strongman, notice the moment you need the last word or the room's agreement, and let it go, on purpose, without collapsing. If you tend toward the passive man, notice the moment you go silent to avoid conflict, and say the true thing, kindly and out loud. Do not announce either as growth. Just do the harder thing and write down what you were actually afraid of when you did it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you made us men on purpose, and you placed the first man in a garden to work it and to keep it before you ever said a word about who was in charge. Forgive us the caricatures we swallowed, the strongman who is only a scared boy shouting and the passive man who calls his absence peace. We have used volume to hide fear and silence to hide the same fear. Teach us the strength that is a roof and not a storm, the courage that shows up and the humility that does not need to win. Make us men whose strength the people around us can rest under. And where we never had a man to show us, be the Father who does. Amen.
reflection: Which caricature of manhood did I inherit, and how much of my behavior is still a performance of it?
Where have I called my passivity humility, or my domination leadership, to avoid seeing either for what it is?
What is my strength actually for, and would the people closest to me say they feel sheltered by it or braced against it?
sessions.teaching: A young man sat across from Bell and said, with more honesty than most men manage, that he did not know how to be a man, because everyone who had ever tried to tell him was selling something. One set of voices told him a real man dominates, wins, never backs down, takes what he wants and calls the taking strength. The other set told him the whole idea of manhood was toxic and he should more or less apologize for having shoulders. He was standing exactly in the middle of the culture war over masculinity, being handed two cartoons, and it had not occurred to anyone that neither cartoon was going to make him a man. So we begin there, because the real question is not which side of that war to enlist in. The real question is what manhood is actually for, and you cannot grow into a thing you have only ever seen drawn as a caricature. Notice where Scripture starts, because it is not where either side starts. It does not open with conquest, with the warrior or the king or the man who takes. It opens with a garden and a man placed inside it to work it and to keep it, given labor and given responsibility before any culture had written him a single line of script. The first thing said over a man is not dominate. It is cultivate and protect. Take the strong case for the recovery of masculine strength first, because it is making a real point against a real failure. A whole shelf of books and a whole chorus of voices have risen up to say that men were made for weight and risk and burden, that the church has too often turned out men who are merely harmless, domesticated, safe, and useless, and that a man with no strength to offer is not gentle, he is just absent. There is truth in this that the softer voices need to hear, because the very first failure of manhood in the Bible is not Cain's violence. It is Adam's silence. The serpent works on Eve while the man is, the text says, right there with her, and he says nothing, does nothing, protects nothing, and then eats. The original sin of manhood is passivity, a man who was present and might as well not have been. So the recovery movement is not wrong that the passive man is a problem. But watch what keeps happening to that movement, because it slides, almost every time, straight into the caricature it set out to correct. The call to strength curdles into a permit for temper. The call to leadership curdles into the demand to be in charge. The call to courage curdles into the man who can never be crossed, who reads every disagreement as disrespect, who mistakes volume for authority and getting his way for godliness. And here is where I have to stand inside it, because I know both counterfeits from the inside. Raised without a father, I had no template, so I built one out of whatever looked like strength, and for years the thing that looked most like strength to me was control, the managed room, the winning argument, the anger that felt more like power than the truth ever did. I have also gone the other way, gone silent and passive and called it keeping the peace, when it was really just Adam in the garden again, present and useless, letting the thing go wrong because speaking up felt like too much risk. Now the reversal, and it cuts against both sides at once. The loudest counterfeit of manhood and the quietest counterfeit are the same counterfeit underneath, because both are driven by fear. The strongman is terrified of looking weak, so he shouts. The passive man is terrified of the risk of manhood, so he vanishes. Neither one is strong. Real manhood is neither the strongman nor the nice guy, and it is not a blend of the two, a little dominance softened with a little niceness. It is a different thing entirely. It is strength given a purpose outside itself. The man in the garden is strong the way a roof is strong, not so that everyone can admire the roof, but so that something underneath it stays dry. His strength is not for winning and it is not for hiding. It is for working and keeping, for cultivating what has been entrusted to him and protecting it at cost. Paul says it in one breath that neither caricature can survive. Act like men, be strong. And then, before you can pump your fist, let all that you do be done in love. The strength and the love are commanded in the same sentence, and any manhood that keeps only one of them has already become a lie.

Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, steadfastness, gentleness. Paul's charge to a young man he is mentoring lists gentleness among the marks to pursue, naming the very quality the strongman despises as one a real man chases. Gentleness here is strength under command, not weakness.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the history the session only gestures at, because the confusion men feel now is not timeless, it has a datable origin worth tracing. For most of human history a boy learned manhood at his father's side, apprenticed daily to the man's work, whether field or forge or shop, so that becoming a man was a slow transfer watched up close. Nancy Pearcey, in her recent history of the subject, traces how the Industrial Revolution moved work out of the home and sent fathers away to the factory for the first time, breaking that daily apprenticeship and leaving boys to assemble manhood from peers, and later from screens, rather than from men. A group can weigh this carefully, because it explains a great deal about why manhood came to be performed rather than received, proven against other boys rather than handed down by a father. Set this beside the secular men's movement that Robert Bly named in 1990, which grieved the father wound and the loss of male initiation and reached back for myth to fill the hole, getting the ache exactly right even where the answer went astray. Then take the harder theological turn. Charles Taylor described the modern buffered self, the individual sealed off and self-defining, and notice how a manhood with no father to receive it and no purpose outside itself becomes exactly that, a self that must generate its own meaning by performance, which is why the strongman must keep proving and the passive man must keep hiding. Both are the buffered self trying to be a man alone. The aim is not to despise the longing for strong men, which is good and God-given, but to see how a culture broke the handing-down of manhood and then wondered why its men were either brittle or absent, and to ask where that break has shaped your own picture without your consent.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in your group is respected, capable, and quietly proud that he is not like the angry, domineering men he grew up around. He is gentle, agreeable, slow to make waves, and he hears the session on the strongman with obvious relief, sure it is not about him. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor him before it turns him. He is right that he has avoided a real sin, and the refusal of domination is a genuine grace worth naming. But notice how quickly he located the whole danger in the other caricature, because the session had a second half he skipped past, the passive man who calls his absence peace. His gentleness may be the fruit of the Spirit, and it may also be, in places, the old fear of conflict wearing a nicer name, the man who keeps the peace by never showing up to the fight that needed him. Do not let him bank the whole session as a critique of men who are not in the room. Honor the real virtue in him, and still ask, gently, where his agreeableness has become a way of not risking anything, and whether the people who depend on him have ever needed him to be strong and found him quietly gone.

sessions.title: The Father Wound and the God Who Fathers the Fatherless
sessions.aim: To name the father wound honestly, the mark left by a father who was absent, or present and cold, or present and cruel, and to bring it under the God who names himself Father of the fatherless, refusing both the bitterness that stays in the wound and the denial that pretends it left no mark, and pointing to the healing that comes from being fathered by God rather than from finally getting from the father what he never gave.
sessions.summary: Bell writes this one from the inside, because he was raised without a father, and he says the wound a missing father leaves does not announce itself. It hides. It shows up decades later as a hunger for approval that no achievement satisfies, as a rage that surprises you, as a suspicion that you are on your own and always were. The real question is not whether a man was wounded by his father, because nearly every man was, in one of the three ways, the father who left, the father who was there but cold, or the father who was there and cruel. The real question is what he does with the wound. Bell takes the strong case for simply moving on, the manly refusal to blame your father for your life, the conviction that dwelling on it is self-pity and a real man just gets over it. There is something true in it, because bitterness is a real trap and blame can become a whole identity. But the wound you refuse to name does not heal. It goes underground and runs your life from there, and the man most controlled by his father is often the one who insists his father does not matter. Then Bell turns to the strangest and most tender thing, that God does not offer men a technique for father wounds. He offers himself as a Father. Father of the fatherless, the psalm says, and it does not mean God will help you find closure with the man who failed you. It means God moves into the empty chair. Then the reversal. The healing is not getting from your earthly father, at last, what he never gave, because most men never will. The healing is being fathered by God now, receiving the approval you were starving for as a gift you did not earn, so that you can finally stop demanding it from a man who cannot give it, living or dead.

keyScripture.why: Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation, naming God as the one who takes up the specific role a missing or failing father left empty, not as a distant deity but as a Father who moves into the vacant place and defends the ones no one else defended.

discussion.q: Bell says nearly every man carries a father wound in one of three forms, the father who left, the father who was cold, or the father who was cruel. Without performing and without blaming, what was your father to you, and what did his version leave in you?
discussion.behind: Open the tenderest door of the whole study, and open it carefully. Men will want to defend their fathers or dismiss the question. Give permission to be honest without disloyalty, to say the father was loved and still left a mark. Do not rush anyone. The goal is not to indict fathers but to name honestly what was there and what was missing, so it can be brought into the light.

discussion.q: Bell says the father wound does not announce itself but shows up decades later as a hunger for approval, a surprising rage, or a certainty that you are on your own. Where do you see the old wound running your adult life without your permission?
discussion.behind: Move from the past to the present, because the point is not the history but its grip now. Help men connect the buried thing to the visible pattern, the workaholism chasing an approval that never comes, the anger out of proportion to the moment, the refusal to depend on anyone. The wound you cannot name is the one still driving. Go first and name yours.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that a real man just gets over it and does not blame his father for his life. What is true in that, and where does refusing to name the wound become the very thing that keeps it in control of you?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. Bitterness and blame are real traps, and endless grievance is not healing. But the manly refusal to look at the wound is not strength, it is avoidance, and the man most run by his father is often the one who insists his father does not matter. Help the room see the difference between naming a wound to heal it and nursing a wound to excuse yourself.

discussion.q: Psalm 68 calls God the Father of the fatherless, and Bell says this means God moves into the empty chair rather than helping you get closure with the man who failed you. What is your honest reaction to being fathered by God, and what makes it hard to receive?
discussion.behind: This is the theological center, and it is hard for men to receive, not just to understand. Some had fathers so bad that the word Father is damaged. Handle that with care. The point is not that God is a better version of your dad but that God is a Father whose approval you never have to earn and can never lose. Let men sit with why that is so hard to believe about themselves.

discussion.q: Bell says the healing is not finally getting from your earthly father what he never gave, because most men never will, but being fathered by God now. Who are you still waiting on for an approval you will never get, and what would it free you to do if you stopped waiting?
discussion.behind: Close on the reversal and the freedom in it. Many men are organizing their whole lives around a verdict from a father who is unable or unwilling or no longer alive to give it. Name that gently. The gospel offer is that the approval you were starving for is already given in Christ, so you can stop auditioning. Let the room feel the release, not as closure with the father but as being fathered by God.

objections.objection: All this father wound talk is just an excuse. Plenty of men had bad fathers and turned out fine, and blaming your dad for who you are now is weak and self-pitying. At some point you are a grown man responsible for yourself.
objections.response: Grant the part that is guarding something true, because it is guarding responsibility, and responsibility matters. A man is accountable for what he does with his life, no father's failure excuses cruelty or cowardice, and a grievance nursed into an identity is its own kind of chain. So the fear of self-pity is not foolish. But hear the distinction the objection misses, because naming a wound is not the same as blaming it. You can take full responsibility for your life and still tell the truth about what shaped it, and in fact you cannot take responsibility for a wound you refuse to look at, because the unnamed wound runs you from underground, unaccountable, invisible. The manly refusal to look at it is not strength, it is a man handing his father the steering wheel and insisting he is driving. Real responsibility begins with honesty, and the strongest thing a man can do with a father wound is name it in the light and bring it to God, not pretend a grown man does not have one.

objections.objection: If God is a father, that does not help me, it makes it worse, because my father is exactly why I want nothing to do with the word. Telling me God is a Father just puts the face of the man who hurt me on the God I am supposed to trust.
objections.response: Take this with complete seriousness, because for a man whose father was absent or cold or cruel, the word Father is not neutral, it is a wound, and anyone who says God is a father as if that automatically comforts has not sat with your pain. So hear it carefully. Scripture does not say God is like your father only bigger. It says God is the Father your father was meant to point to and failed to, the reality your earthly father was a broken copy of, sometimes a copy so broken it obscured the original entirely. When Jesus reveals the Father, he shows a father who runs to the son who wasted everything, who is moved with compassion, who is gentle and lowly in heart. The point is not to project your father onto God. It is that God offers to heal the very word your father damaged, to be the Father who does not leave, does not go cold, does not turn cruel, so that the name that was a wound can slowly become the place you are finally safe.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Whose approval are you still, at your age, quietly organizing your life to win, and what would change if you truly believed you already had a Father who was pleased with you?
sessions.practice: This week, do two things privately. First, name your father wound to God plainly, out loud if you can, without performing and without blaming, just telling the truth about what was there and what was missing. Second, when you catch yourself chasing the old approval, in your work, in a room, in the mirror, stop and say to yourself that you already have a Father, and that his verdict over you in Christ is settled and cannot be earned or lost. Write down what rises in you the first time you try to believe it.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father of the fatherless, you know exactly what was and was not at the head of each of our tables, the chair that was empty, the man who was there but far away, the one who was there and dangerous. We have carried the wound for decades and called it nothing, and it has run us the whole time, chasing an approval that never came, braced for a blow, sure we were on our own. You are not a bigger version of the man who failed us. You are the Father he was meant to show us and could not. Move into the empty chair. Say over us the word we spent our lives trying to earn. And let us, who were fathered by grace, become men who father, so that the wound stops here. Amen.
reflection: What exactly was my father wound, the absence, the coldness, or the cruelty, and have I ever named it honestly instead of defending or dismissing it?
Where is the old wound still driving, in my hunger for approval, my surprising anger, or my refusal to depend on anyone?
Do I actually believe God offers to be my Father now, and what in me resists receiving an approval I did not earn and cannot lose?
sessions.teaching: Bell writes this session from the inside, and he says so plainly, because he was raised without a father, and a man should tell you where he is standing before he talks about a thing like this. He grew up with an empty chair at the head of the table, and he learned early what he now wants every man in the room to hear, that the wound a missing father leaves does not announce itself. It does not walk up and introduce itself as a father wound. It hides. It buries itself so deep that a man can go thirty years insisting he is fine, that his father did not matter, that he never thinks about it, and be telling the truth as far as he can see, while the wound runs his entire life from underground. It surfaces, decades later, in disguise. It shows up as a hunger for approval that no achievement ever satisfies, the promotion that should have been enough and was not, the applause that emptied out by morning. It shows up as a rage that surprises you, an anger out of all proportion to the small thing that triggered it, because the small thing brushed against the old thing. It shows up as a bone-deep certainty that you are on your own, that no one is coming, that you had better handle it yourself because that is how it has always been. So the real question of this session is not whether you were wounded by your father, because very nearly every man was, in one of three ways. There is the father who left, by divorce or death or the door, the empty chair. There is the father who was physically present and emotionally absent, there at the table and a thousand miles away behind his eyes, the cold father. And there is the father who was present and cruel, whose attention was worse than his absence would have been. Almost every man is somewhere in those three. The real question is what a man does with the wound. Take the strong case for just getting over it, because it sounds like strength and it is what most men were taught. A real man, the reasoning goes, does not blame his father for his life. Dwelling on it is self-pity, and self-pity is contemptible, and the manly thing is to shrug it off, take responsibility, and move on. There is something true in this, and I want to grant it fully, because bitterness is a real trap and blame can metastasize into an entire identity, a man who explains his every failure by pointing back at his dad and never grows up. That man exists and he is not free either. But watch the lie folded into the manly refusal, because the wound you refuse to name does not heal. It does not go away when you stop looking at it. It goes underground, and from underground it runs the show, unaccountable and invisible, and the man most completely controlled by his father is very often the one who insists, with real conviction, that his father does not matter to him at all. I know this because I lived it. I told myself for years that growing up without a father had made me strong, self-reliant, that it was a fact about my past and nothing more, and the whole time it was shaping how I led, how I loved, how desperately I needed to be respected, how hard it was for me to depend on anyone or believe anyone would stay. Now the tender turn, the strangest and best thing in the session. God does not respond to the father wound with a technique. He does not hand men a five-step process for closure with the man who failed them. He does something far more personal and far more scandalous. He offers himself as a Father. Father of the fatherless, the psalm says, and read it slowly, because it does not say God will help you find peace about your absent dad from a comfortable distance. It says God moves into the empty chair. He takes up the specific, vacant role. He fathers the fatherless, not metaphorically but actually, becoming to the abandoned the thing they were abandoned by. And here is the reversal that heals, if a man can receive it. The healing you are looking for is not getting from your earthly father, at long last, the thing he never gave you, because the hard truth is that most men never will. The father who could not say it at thirty will not say it at seventy, and many of the fathers are dead, and the reconciliation you have been waiting for is not coming in the form you wanted. If your healing depends on that, you will wait your whole life. But the gospel offers something better than the closure you cannot get. It offers to father you now. It offers the approval you have been starving for since you were a boy, not as a wage you finally earn but as a gift already given, the Father in heaven looking at you in Christ and saying the words you spent your life auditioning for, this is my beloved son. And when a man begins, even slowly, to believe that, something loosens. He can stop demanding from a man, living or dead, an approval that man was never able to give, because he is being fathered at last by the One who can.

scriptureStudy.note: Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation. God names himself by the very role the missing father left empty. This is not a distant deity but a Father who moves into the vacant chair and defends the ones no one else defended.

For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in. Scripture names the abandonment without softening it and then answers it, not with a technique for closure but with a God who takes in the very one the parents put out.

But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him. Jesus reveals the Father as one who runs to the son who wasted everything, undoing the picture of the cold or cruel father and replacing it with a Father moved to compassion at the first sight of a son coming home.

You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, Abba! Father! The wound of fatherlessness is answered by adoption, a legal and permanent sonship, and by a Spirit who teaches the fatherless to use the intimate name for God the very father wound made hardest to say.

See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God. John marvels at the sheer kind of love that makes the fatherless into children of God, an identity given rather than earned, which is exactly the approval the wounded man keeps trying to work for.

I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty. God states the offer directly, promising to be a father to those who come to him, taking up the role in the first person as a covenant commitment, not a comforting image.

This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased. The Father speaks this over Jesus before a single miracle, before the ministry begins, and in Christ the same verdict falls on the adopted son, the approval spoken before the work, which is the exact opposite of the wage the wounded man keeps trying to earn.

sessions.goingDeeper: Take up the research on fatherlessness honestly, and test it against Scripture rather than swallowing it whole or dismissing it for its source. The social science on father absence is sobering and broadly agreed, that children raised without an involved father are at markedly higher risk across a range of outcomes, and Warren Farrell, in his recent work on the boy crisis, has gathered much of this data to argue that father absence is among the most under-discussed drivers of male struggle. A group should grant the finding its weight, because it confirms in numbers what Scripture assumed in narrative, that a father matters enormously and his absence leaves a real and measurable mark. But notice what the data can and cannot do. It can name the symptom, the wound, the cost, with real precision, and it cannot supply the cure, because no statistic can father a fatherless man. That is where the secular account runs out and the gospel begins. Set the research beside the secular men's work of Robert Bly and the mythopoetic movement, which grieved the father wound genuinely and reached back to myth and ritual to try to fill it, getting the ache right while missing where the healing actually comes from. Then press the hardest and most pastoral turn, the theological one. If the deepest father wound is healed not by finding the earthly father but by being fathered by God, then the doctrine of adoption is not a dry legal footnote but the most personally urgent truth in the New Testament for a wounded man, the announcement that the fatherless are made sons, permanently, by grace. A group should sit with the difference between closure, which the world offers and often cannot deliver, and adoption, which God offers and has already delivered in Christ. And it should be handled with pastoral care, because in almost any group of men there is one whose wound is fresh or severe, and the aim is never to rush a man past his grief into a slogan, but to let the God who names himself Father of the fatherless be, slowly, exactly that.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in your group speaks warmly about his father, insists they had a great relationship, and grows visibly impatient with the whole premise of a father wound, calling it a therapy fad that lets weak men off the hook. He is not lying, and he may well have had a genuinely good father. Here is the careful work for the leader, and it requires honoring him without simply agreeing. Some men truly were well fathered, and the study should be glad for it and not manufacture a wound where there is none. But notice the heat, because the intensity of his impatience is worth a gentle question, since a man who was securely fathered rarely needs to attack the idea that others were not. His reaction may guard a real gift, or it may guard a wound so defended he cannot look at it, the loyalty that will not let him say a true and hard thing about a father he loves. Do not pry, and do not insist he is wounded when he may not be. Honor the good father if there was one, and still leave the door open, gently, by asking whether his certainty is peace or armor, and letting him know the room is safe if he ever wants to set the armor down.

sessions.title: Strength Under Control, the Man Jesus Was
sessions.aim: To hold up Jesus as the true measure of manhood, the man who wept openly, knelt to wash feet, and drove the money changers out with a whip, and to define strength not as the absence of feeling or the presence of force but as power entirely under command, refusing both the caricature that makes Jesus soft and the caricature that makes the whip a permit for a man's temper.
sessions.summary: Bell says the reason men cannot agree on what strength is is that they have never looked long enough at the one man who had all of it. We argue about masculinity in the abstract and skip the concrete case standing in front of us, Jesus, who does not fit either team's cartoon. The team that wants a soft, gentle, harmless Jesus has to explain the whip and the overturned tables. The team that wants a warrior Jesus who never showed weakness has to explain the tears, the basin, the towel. The real question is what strength actually is, and Jesus answers it not with a definition but with a life. He wept, publicly, at a friend's grave, and no one who watched him thought he was weak. He knelt in front of his own followers and washed the road-filth off their feet, taking the slave's job, and it was the strongest thing in the room. And he made a whip and drove the money changers out of the temple, and that was not a loss of control, it was strength aimed with perfect precision at exactly the right target. Bell takes the strong case for the warrior reading, the men who love the whip and quote it against a church they find too soft. There is truth in it, because Jesus was not harmless and a manhood with no capacity for holy anger is not Christlike either. But the whip is where the strongman gets exposed, because Jesus was angry at injustice done to others, in God's house, and never once at an insult to himself. Then the reversal. Strength is not the absence of feeling, or Jesus was weak when he wept, and it is not the presence of force, or Jesus was strong only with the whip. Strength is power under control, every ounce of it available and every ounce of it aimed at the good of others rather than the defense of self. The man who could call down legions chose the nails. That is the measure, and no other passes.

keyScripture.why: Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city, ranking the man who governs his own spirit above the conqueror, and naming self-command, not force, as the higher strength, which is precisely the strength the man Jesus embodied.

discussion.q: Bell says both teams in the masculinity debate have a Jesus they cannot explain, the soft team has the whip and the warrior team has the tears. Which of those two is harder for you to fit into your picture of a strong man, and why?
discussion.behind: Open by exposing each man's default Jesus. Most men have quietly edited Jesus down to the half that confirms their existing picture of strength. Help the room notice which half they skip, the weeping or the whip, because the half you cannot explain is usually the half your idea of manhood most needs. Do not resolve it yet, just surface the edited Jesus.

discussion.q: Jesus wept openly at a friend's grave and no one thought him weak. Where did you learn that a strong man does not show what he feels, and what has that lesson cost you?
discussion.behind: Press on the tears and the buried teaching underneath. Most men were trained early that feeling is weakness and composure is strength, and the training runs deep. Help men connect the lesson to its cost, the numbness, the isolation, the sons watching a father who never lets them see anything. Jesus wept in public and lost no strength doing it. Go first if the room is guarded.

discussion.q: Jesus knelt and washed his followers' feet, taking the slave's job, and Bell calls it the strongest thing in the room. Why is it so hard for men to believe that the lowest service is a form of strength rather than a loss of standing?
discussion.behind: Move to the basin and the fear under it. Men are trained to protect their standing, and voluntary lowliness reads as losing rank. Help the room see that only the truly secure man can kneel, that Jesus washed feet precisely because he knew who he was, and that the fear of looking low is the strongman's tell. Ask where each man refuses the low service that would actually serve.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case for the men who love the whip and quote it against a soft church, and grants that Jesus was not harmless. What is true in that, and where does the whip get misused to justify a man's temper?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves carefully, because this is where the session can go wrong. Holy anger is real, and a manhood with no capacity for it is not Christlike. But the whip was aimed at injustice done to others in God's house, never at an insult to Jesus himself, and that distinction is everything. Help the room test their own anger by it, since the strongman's anger is almost always about himself.

discussion.q: Bell says strength is not the absence of feeling or the presence of force, but power under control, and that the man who could call down legions chose the nails. Where in your life is your strength aimed at defending yourself rather than serving others, and what would it look like to aim it the way Jesus did?
discussion.behind: Land on the definition and make it personal. The whole session comes to rest here, that strength is power under command, aimed at the good of others rather than the defense of self. Push each man to locate where his strength currently serves his own defense, his reputation, his comfort, his being right, and to imagine it re-aimed. End on the cross as the measure, power fully held and fully given.

objections.objection: You are just giving me the soft Jesus, the gentle, feelings-first Jesus that the church already overuses. Men need a Jesus with a spine, and turning strength into washing feet and crying is exactly why the church has no men left in it.
objections.response: Refuse the false choice, because this objection has cut Jesus in half and kept the wrong lesson from the half it likes. The Jesus in this session is not the soft Jesus, he is the whole one, the same man who wept at the grave and made a whip and cleared the temple, and any picture that keeps only the whip is as edited as the one that keeps only the tears. So grant the real point, that Jesus had a spine, that he was not harmless, that a limp and feelings-only Christ is a distortion the church does overuse. But notice what the whip actually was, aimed at real injustice, in God's house, on behalf of others, and never once swung to defend his own honor when he was mocked and beaten and spat on and stayed silent. That is not a man with no spine. That is a man with total power under total control, which is a far higher and far rarer strength than the man who cannot take an insult. The problem with the church is not that it made Jesus too gentle. It is that it keeps letting angry men quote the whip while skipping the silence before Pilate.

objections.objection: So a real man is supposed to be emotional and cry and serve everyone. That just sounds like being a pushover with extra steps, and pushovers get walked on and cannot protect anyone.
objections.response: Hear the fear, because it is pointing at something real, since a man who is only soft, who cannot stand firm or protect or say the hard true thing, is not Christlike either, and the passive man is a genuine failure the study has already named. But you have confused two different things, being under control with being controllable, and they are opposites. Jesus wept, and no one walked over him. He washed feet, and then he faced down the powers of his day and went to a cross on purpose, in command of every moment of it. The strength here is not the absence of steel, it is steel that answers only to God and never to the man's own ego. A pushover is run by his fear of conflict. Jesus was run by his Father's will, which is why he could be gentle without being weak and fierce without being cruel. The goal is not to make you soft. It is to put your strength under the one command that makes it safe, so that you protect what should be protected and never wound to defend yourself.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When your strength comes out as anger, is it ever like the whip in the temple, aimed at real injustice done to others, or is it almost always about an insult to you?
sessions.practice: This week, run your strength through the test Jesus sets. When anger rises, pause and ask one question, is this about injustice to someone else, or an insult to me, and let the answer govern what you do next. And find one place to take the basin, one low, unseen service you would normally consider beneath you, and do it deliberately, the way a man does a strong thing. Write down what it exposed in you, the anger that turned out to be about your own ego, or the fear that made kneeling feel like losing.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you are the man we keep editing, because the whole of you will not fit the cartoons we prefer. You wept at a grave and lost no strength. You knelt with a basin and were the strongest one in the room. You made a whip for the injustice done in your Father's house and stayed silent when they struck your own face. Forgive us the strength we aim at our own defense, the anger that is only ever about us, the composure we mistake for courage, the standing we are too afraid to lay down. Teach us power under your command, every ounce of it held and every ounce of it given for others, the way you held yours all the way to the nails you could have refused. Make us strong the way you are strong. Amen.
reflection: Which half of Jesus do I edit out, the one who wept or the one who wielded the whip, and what does that tell me about my own idea of strength?
Where is my anger really about an insult to me rather than an injustice to someone else, and what would it take to tell the difference in the moment?
Is my strength under control, answering to God, or is it controllable, run by my fear of conflict or my need to defend myself?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the reason men cannot agree on what strength is is that they keep arguing about it in the abstract and never look long enough at the one man who actually had all of it. We debate masculinity in theory, trade slogans and caricatures, and walk right past the concrete case standing in front of us the whole time, which is Jesus, a man, fully a man, who stubbornly refuses to fit either team's cartoon. Consider what each side has to do to keep him. The team that wants a soft Jesus, gentle and harmless and mostly agreeable, has to quietly lose an entire scene, the day he sat down and braided cords into a whip and drove men and animals out of the temple and flipped the tables and poured the coins across the floor. That happened. It is in all four Gospels in one form or another. The soft Jesus cannot survive it. But the team that wants the warrior Jesus, the alpha who never showed weakness and never bent, has an even bigger problem, because that Jesus wept. He stood at the grave of his friend Lazarus, in front of a crowd, and cried, and the shortest verse in the Bible records it without embarrassment, Jesus wept. And that same Jesus knelt down on the floor in front of his own followers, took off his outer garment, wrapped a towel around his waist like a household slave, and washed the road-filth and the animal-filth off their feet, one pair at a time, including the feet of the man he knew was about to sell him. So the real question, the one this whole study has been circling, gets its answer here, and the answer is not a definition. It is a life. What is strength. Jesus wept, publicly, and not one person who watched him thought, there goes a weak man. He knelt and washed feet, took the lowest job in the house, and it was, Bell insists, the strongest thing in the room, because only a man who is completely secure in who he is can go that low on purpose. And he made a whip and cleared the temple, and that was not a man losing control. Read it carefully. It was strength aimed with surgical precision at exactly the right target, holy anger at real injustice, and it stopped exactly where it should. Take the strong case for the men who love the whip, because they are making a point the soft church needs to hear. There is a whole tribe of men who quote the temple cleansing against a Christianity they experience as limp, feminized, allergic to any strength at all, and they are not entirely wrong. Jesus was not harmless. A manhood with no capacity for anger at evil is not more Christlike than an angry one, it is less, because it cannot be moved by the things that move the heart of God. Grant that fully. But here is where the whip exposes the strongman instead of endorsing him, and it is the hinge of the entire session. Look at what Jesus was angry about. He was angry at injustice done to others, at the poor being fleeced in God's own house, at the place of prayer for all nations turned into a den of robbers. He was never once angry, with whip or word, at an insult to himself. When they mocked him, he was silent. When they beat him, he did not retaliate. When they nailed him up and gambled for his clothes, he asked the Father to forgive them. The same man, the same strength, and it never fired in his own defense, not once. And I have to sit down inside that, because my anger is almost never like the whip. My anger is almost always about me, my honor, my being disrespected, my will crossed, and then I reach for the temple story to make my temper holy, which is exactly the theft the whip was driving out. Now the reversal, the definition the whole session was built to reach. Strength is not the absence of feeling, because if it were, Jesus was weak at the grave. And strength is not the presence of force, because if it were, Jesus was strong only for the few minutes he held the whip and weak every other hour of his life. Strength is neither. Strength is power under control, every ounce of it available and every ounce of it aimed, not at the defense of the self, but at the good of others and the glory of God. It is the whole capacity to act, fully present, fully governed. And the picture of it is not the whip. It is the garden, where a man who says he could call on twelve legions of angels, who has every power there is, tells his friend to put the sword away and holds out his hands for the ropes. He had all the strength. He chose the nails. That is the measure of a man, and when you lay every other version of masculinity against it, the strongman and the passive man and every cartoon in between, not one of them passes.

scriptureStudy.note: Jesus wept. The shortest verse in the Bible records the strongest man who ever lived crying openly at a friend's grave, and it is recorded without apology or embarrassment. Feeling deeply and showing it cost Jesus none of his strength, which unmakes the lesson that a man hides what he feels.

If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. Jesus takes the slave's task in front of his own followers and then commands them to do the same, defining greatness downward, so that the lowest service becomes the mark of the highest security.

Making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple. The cleansing is real and fierce, and it forbids any soft, harmless Jesus, but the anger is aimed at injustice done to others in God's house, precise and purposeful, never a tantrum and never a defense of his own honor.

He who rules his spirit is better than he who takes a city. Scripture ranks the man who governs his own spirit above the conqueror, naming self-command as the higher strength, the exact quality the strongman lacks and the man Jesus embodied fully.

Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart. Jesus describes his own heart, the deepest thing about him, as gentle and lowly, so gentleness is not a concession to weakness but the character of the strongest man, freely chosen from a position of total power.

Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? At the moment of arrest Jesus names the full power available to him and then declines it, which is the definition of strength under control, capacity fully present and fully surrendered to the Father's will.

A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench. The prophet's picture of the coming servant is of overwhelming strength that handles the fragile with total gentleness, power so complete it can be trusted with what is nearly broken, which is the strength this session is after.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the deeper structure of what strength under control actually is, because the phrase is easy to say and hard to live, and Scripture and history both illumine it. The classical and Christian traditions had a word for exactly this, the virtue the older writers called temperance or self-mastery, not the modern sense of abstaining from pleasure but the fuller sense of a man whose passions answer to his reason and his reason to God, so that his whole force is available and none of it runs him. A group can weigh how far this has been lost, since the modern picture of the authentic man is precisely the one who does not rule his passions but expresses them, follows his anger and his appetite wherever they lead and calls the following freedom, when the older wisdom would call it slavery. Set this beside Dane Ortlund's recent recovery of Matthew 11 and the heart of Christ as gentle and lowly, a reminder that the deepest thing about the strongest man was not force but tenderness, freely given from unassailable security. Then take the hard cultural turn. Our moment produces strongman influencers, men who market a masculinity of dominance, appetite, and the refusal ever to be crossed, and they are compelling to young men precisely because they offer a counterfeit of strength that is really just passion off the leash, and a group should be able to name honestly both why the appeal is real, the hunger for strength is God-given, and why the offer is a lie, because a man ruled by his anger and his appetite is not powerful, he is possessed by the very things he thinks he commands. The measure that exposes every counterfeit is the same, the man who could call twelve legions and chose the nails, whose every capacity was intact and whose every capacity answered to his Father. The aim is to recover strength under control as the true and difficult masculine virtue, neither the suppression of feeling nor its indulgence, but its government, under God, for the good of others.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in your group is admired for being unflappable, the one who never loses his temper, never raises his voice, never lets anyone see him rattled, and he takes real pride in it as his particular strength. When the session names strength as power under control, he assumes it is describing him. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor the genuine virtue before it probes. His self-command may be exactly the strength the session commends, and if it is, say so. But notice the session had two edges, and the whip was one of them, so ask which kind of control he actually has. There is the control of a man whose strength answers to God and is fully available when injustice calls for it, and there is the control of a man who has simply gone numb, who never gets angry because he never lets himself feel anything, whose calm is not mastery but absence. The first can weep at a grave and clear a temple. The second cannot do either, and mistakes his flatness for peace. Do not assume you know which he is. Honor the discipline if it is real, and still ask, gently, whether his composure has ever broken for the right reason, whether he can be moved by injustice done to others, or whether the same wall that keeps his anger in also keeps his heart out.
